cards.front: Capsaicin, the molecule in chili peppers, carries no heat. Why does it feel hot?
cards.back: Capsaicin opens TRPV1, the same channel noxious heat opens, so it excites the same sensory neurons and the brain receives a similar message from both.
cards.why: The burn is not a temperature reading. The neurons' firing says which line is active and carries information about strength and timing, but does not uniquely identify whether capsaicin or heat drove it.
cards.quote: Capsaicin opens TRPV1 and excites sensory neurons that noxious heat also excites, so the brain receives a similar message from both.

cards.front: What is the difference between nociception and pain?
cards.back: Nociception is the neural encoding of a damaging or potentially damaging stimulus. Pain is an experience.
cards.why: A firing nociceptor or a withdrawing mouse paw is evidence about nociception, not a report of pain.
cards.quote: Nociception is the neural encoding of a damaging or potentially damaging stimulus.
cards.section: What the skin is measuring

cards.front: Under the 'follow the line' idea for touch and pain, what does a sensory neuron's firing tell the brain, and what can it not tell?
cards.back: It tells which line is active, with information about the input's strength and timing. It does not uniquely identify what activated it; the channels and structure of its endings decide what can.
cards.quote: it does not uniquely identify what activated it: the channels and structure of its endings decide what can.
cards.section: What the skin is measuring

cards.front: Nociceptors end as {{c1::free nerve endings}}, so transduction happens in the terminal membrane.
cards.quote: Nociceptors, the sensory neurons that carry out nociception, end as free nerve endings, so transduction happens in the terminal membrane.
cards.section: What a line reports: the channels

cards.front: To find the capsaicin receptor, rodent dorsal root ganglion cDNA was expressed in pools in HEK293 cells. Why HEK293 cells, and what was the readout?
cards.back: HEK293 cells do not normally respond to capsaicin, so a response had to come from the added cDNA. The readout was capsaicin-evoked calcium influx; positive pools were divided down to one cDNA, VR1 (now TRPV1).
cards.quote: They expressed it in pools in HEK293 cells, which do not normally respond to capsaicin, and screened for capsaicin-evoked calcium influx.
cards.section: What a line reports: the channels

cards.front: Which three kinds of stimulus activate TRPV1?
cards.back: Capsaicin, noxious heat and protons.
cards.why: The cloned rat channel in foreign cells opened with heat above about 43 °C, a property of that channel, not of human perception.
cards.quote: TRPV1 responds to capsaicin, noxious heat and protons.
cards.section: What a line reports: the channels

cards.front: {{c1::TRPM8}} is the menthol receptor, activated by cool-to-cold temperatures.
cards.quote: TRPM8 is the menthol receptor, activated by cool-to-cold temperatures.
cards.section: What a line reports: the channels

cards.front: What activates TRPA1, and how do these agents mainly act on it?
cards.back: Thiol-reactive irritants such as mustard oil. They act mainly by covalently modifying cysteines in its N-terminus, with a lysine also contributing (shown in foreign cells).
cards.quote: TRPA1 is activated by thiol-reactive irritants, such as mustard oil.
cards.section: What a line reports: the channels

cards.front: {{c1::Piezo2}} is a mechanically activated channel needed for gentle touch in mice.
cards.back: Merkel cells in the skin use it too.
cards.quote: Piezo2 is a mechanically activated channel needed for gentle touch in mice
cards.section: What a line reports: the channels

cards.front: A new compound opens a channel that cool temperatures also open, and it mainly drives intact cold-sensitive neurons. Applied to the skin, what will it most likely feel like, and why?
cards.back: Most likely cool, even though the skin does not cool. The neurons it drives report the cold line, whatever opened their channels.
cards.why: Menthol and TRPM8 are the example. Depending on dose and how it is applied, menthol can also sting or burn.
cards.quote: Most likely cool, if the chemical mainly drives intact cold-sensitive neurons.
cards.section: What a line reports: the channels

cards.front: Injured tissue releases protons. Predict how protons change the heat response of cloned TRPV1 channels.
cards.back: Protons lower TRPV1's heat threshold, so milder heat opens it. At pH 5.9 or below, the cloned channel opened at room temperature.
cards.quote: Protons lower its heat threshold, and at pH 5.9 or below the cloned channel opened at room temperature
cards.section: What a line reports: the channels

cards.front: A cDNA from rat sensory neurons makes HEK cells respond to capsaicin and to heat. What does this show about the gene, and what does it not show?
cards.back: It shows the gene is sufficient: enough to give a foreign cell the response. It does not show the gene is necessary in the animal, nor that it is the only heat sensor.
cards.quote: Cloning shows the gene is sufficient: enough to give a foreign cell the response.
cards.section: What a line reports: the channels

cards.front: TRPV1-null mice showed no vanilloid-evoked pain behaviour, a partial deficit in detecting painful heat, little inflammatory heat hypersensitivity, and normal mechanical responses. What two conclusions follow?
cards.back: TRPV1 is needed for capsaicin responses and part of heat sensing, but it is not 'the pain receptor': mechanical responses do not need it. Because the heat deficit was partial, other heat sensors must exist.
cards.quote: The heat deficit was partial, so other heat sensors must exist.
cards.section: What a line reports: the channels

cards.front: TRPM8, cloned as the menthol receptor, gives foreign cells responses to cool temperatures. Design the mouse experiment that tests whether animals need it to sense cold, and say how you would read a partial loss.
cards.back: Knock out TRPM8 and compare knockouts with littermate controls on menthol-evoked behaviour, responses at several cool and cold temperatures, and a mechanical assay as a control modality. A partial loss means TRPM8 is needed for part of cold sensing and other sensors exist.
cards.why: Rests on the sufficiency versus necessity rule and the design used for the TRPV1 knockout: test several temperatures, since a partial loss may appear only at some.
cards.quote: Knock out the gene in mice and compare knockouts with littermate controls on capsaicin-evoked behaviour
cards.section: What a line reports: the channels

cards.front: In the glabrous skin of the human hand, which touch afferents adapt slowly, and what does slow adaptation let them report?
cards.back: Merkel cell (SAI) afferents, with small receptive fields, and SAII afferents, with large ones. They keep firing while a stimulus is held, so they report what is there, such as an edge or a stretch.
cards.quote: Slow adapters keep firing while a stimulus is held, such as an edge or a stretch.
cards.section: What touch afferents report: four receptors, three fibre sizes

cards.front: In the glabrous skin of the human hand, which touch afferents adapt rapidly, and what does rapid adaptation let them report?
cards.back: Meissner corpuscle afferents, with small receptive fields, and Pacinian corpuscle afferents, with large ones. They fire mainly as a stimulus starts and stops, so they report what is changing, such as slip or vibration.
cards.quote: Fast adapters fire mainly as a stimulus starts and stops, as with slip or vibration.
cards.section: What touch afferents report: four receptors, three fibre sizes

cards.front: Of the two rapidly adapting afferents of glabrous skin, which responds best to high-frequency vibration, and which to low-frequency flutter and slip?
cards.back: Pacinian corpuscle afferents respond best to high-frequency vibration, peaking near 250 Hz in reviews of fingertip data. Meissner corpuscle afferents respond best to low-frequency vibration. These are bands of best sensitivity, not cutoffs.
cards.quote: They respond best to high-frequency vibration, with a peak near 250 Hz in reviews of fingertip data.
cards.section: What touch afferents report: four receptors, three fibre sizes

cards.front: A coin is pressed onto a fingertip, held for several seconds, then lifted. Which afferents fire throughout the hold, and which fire only at contact and at lift?
cards.back: Merkel (SAI) afferents under the coin fire throughout, plus SAII afferents if the press stretches the skin. Meissner and Pacinian afferents fire at contact, fall quiet during the hold, and fire again at lift, because lifting is also a change.
cards.quote: The rapidly adapting Meissner and Pacinian afferents fired at contact and fall quiet while the coin is held.
cards.section: What touch afferents report: four receptors, three fibre sizes

cards.front: Raised dots spaced about 0.5 mm apart are pressed onto a fingertip and held still. Which afferent type is best placed to signal the dot pattern during the hold, and why?
cards.back: Merkel cell (SAI) afferents. They adapt slowly, so they keep reporting a held pattern; they have small receptive fields; and single human SAI afferents can resolve spatial detail down to about 0.5 mm.
cards.quote: single human SAI afferents can resolve spatial detail down to about 0.5 mm
cards.section: What touch afferents report: four receptors, three fibre sizes

cards.front: Give the summarised conduction velocities of Aδ and C fibres, and say what these two classes mostly carry.
cards.back: Thinly myelinated Aδ: roughly 5 to 30 m/s. Unmyelinated C: roughly 0.5 to 2 m/s. Together they carry most nociceptive and thermal signals; large myelinated Aβ fibres carry most touch.
cards.quote: Thinly myelinated Aδ fibres, often summarised at roughly 5 to 30 m/s, and unmyelinated C fibres, at roughly 0.5 to 2 m/s
cards.section: What touch afferents report: four receptors, three fibre sizes

cards.front: Is every unmyelinated C fibre a nociceptor? What does the answer imply about using conduction velocity to infer what a fibre reports?
cards.back: No. Some C fibres are low-threshold touch afferents (C-LTMRs), not nociceptors. So speed alone does not fix what a fibre reports.
cards.quote: Most, not all: some C fibres are low-threshold touch afferents (C-LTMRs), not nociceptors.
cards.section: What touch afferents report: four receptors, three fibre sizes

cards.front: Assume constant velocity and conduction alone over a 0.80 m path from foot to cord. How long does an Aβ fibre at 50 m/s take, how long does a C fibre at 1.0 m/s take, and what is the difference?
cards.why: This counts conduction only, leaving out transduction, synapses and central processing.
cards.quote: Take an illustrative path of 1.00 m from foot to cord, and assume constant velocity and conduction alone.
cards.section: What touch afferents report: four receptors, three fibre sizes

cards.front: A skin nerve is stimulated and a recording 0.60 m away shows volleys at 12 ms and 60 ms. Assuming constant speed and conduction alone, what are the two velocities, and which fibre classes fit them?
cards.back: v = L / t. 0.60 m ÷ 0.012 s = 50 m/s, fitting large myelinated Aβ fibres. 0.60 m ÷ 0.060 s = 10 m/s, inside the roughly 5 to 30 m/s range summarised for Aδ fibres.
cards.quote: Axons are also sorted by diameter and myelin, which set conduction velocity: thicker and myelinated means faster
cards.section: What touch afferents report: four receptors, three fibre sizes

cards.front: What does the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway carry, and where does it cross the midline?
cards.back: Fine touch, vibration and position sense from the body. The first-order axon climbs the same-side dorsal column to the gracile or cuneate nucleus; axons from those nuclei cross in the medulla as internal arcuate fibres.
cards.quote: Axons from those nuclei cross the midline as internal arcuate fibres, form the medial lemniscus, and ascend to the thalamus
cards.section: Where each line crosses: two pathways

cards.front: What does the spinothalamic pathway carry, and where does it cross the midline?
cards.back: Pain and temperature. The first-order axon synapses in the dorsal horn near its entry; the second-order axon crosses in the anterior white commissure, reaching the opposite side within a segment or two of entry.
cards.quote: The second-order axon crosses through the anterior white commissure, so the line reaches the opposite side within a segment or two of entry
cards.section: Where each line crosses: two pathways

cards.front: A clean hemisection cuts the left half of the spinal cord at T6. Below the cut, which side loses fine touch and vibration, which side loses pain and temperature, and which side is weak?
cards.back: Left: fine touch, vibration and position sense (dorsal columns not yet crossed) and strength (the lateral corticospinal tract crossed in the medulla). Right: pain and temperature, starting a segment or two below the cut (spinothalamic axons already crossed).
cards.quote: Touch and strength are lost on one side and pain on the other: the Brown-Séquard pattern.
cards.section: Where each line crosses: two pathways

cards.front: After a spinal hemisection, why does pain loss on the opposite side begin one or two segments below the cut rather than at it?
cards.back: Spinothalamic fibres cross a segment or two above their entry. A fibre entering just below the cut may cross above it, reach the far side above the lesion, and be spared.
cards.quote: So the left-sided loss begins one or two segments below the cut, from about T11 to T12 down.
cards.section: Where each line crosses: two pathways

cards.front: A patient with a one-sided spinal cord injury has lost vibration sense in the right leg and pinprick sensation in the left leg. Which half of the cord is damaged, and on what rule?
cards.back: The right half, the side of the vibration loss. Dorsal-column axons run uncrossed in the cord, while spinothalamic axons have already crossed near their entry.
cards.quote: Pain lost on one side and vibration lost on the other point to the half of the cord on the side of the vibration loss.
cards.section: Where each line crosses: two pathways

cards.front: A lesion destroys only the anterior white commissure over spinal segments T4 to T6. Using the crossing rules, predict the sensory deficit.
cards.back: Pain and temperature lost on both sides in a band near those segments, because second-order spinothalamic axons from both sides cross there. Fine touch and vibration are spared, because dorsal-column axons ascend uncrossed and cross in the medulla.
cards.why: Rests on where each line crosses: spinothalamic in the anterior white commissure within a segment or two of entry, dorsal column-medial lemniscus in the medulla.
cards.quote: The second-order axon crosses through the anterior white commissure, so the line reaches the opposite side within a segment or two
cards.section: Where each line crosses: two pathways

cards.front: What is the difference between hyperalgesia and allodynia?
cards.back: Hyperalgesia is greater pain from a normally painful stimulus. Allodynia is pain from a normally innocuous stimulus.
cards.why: Both terms describe the experience, not where the change happens.
cards.quote: Hyperalgesia is greater pain from a normally painful stimulus, like the shower.
cards.section: Turning the report up and down

cards.front: How does tissue injury turn up the nociceptor's report at the ending itself?
cards.back: Injured tissue releases mediators such as bradykinin and protons, which make nociceptors more sensitive (peripheral sensitization).
cards.why: In cultured small sensory neurons from neonatal rats, bradykinin increased the heat-activated inward current, and protein kinase C activators mimicked it.
cards.quote: Injured tissue releases mediators such as bradykinin and protons, which make nociceptors more sensitive.
cards.section: At the ending

cards.front: What is central sensitization?
cards.back: A prolonged but reversible increase in the excitability and synaptic efficacy of central nociceptive neurons, triggered by nociceptor input.
cards.why: It can involve NMDA receptor-mediated rises in postsynaptic calcium.
cards.quote: a prolonged but reversible increase in the excitability and synaptic efficacy of central nociceptive neurons, called central sensitization
cards.section: In the dorsal horn

cards.front: How can convergence of skin and visceral input onto one dorsal horn neuron contribute to referred pain?
cards.back: When one cell hears from both skin and an internal organ, its firing alone does not say which sent the signal, so pain can be felt away from its source.
cards.why: Shown in isolated thoracic cord from 10- to 14-day-old rats (lamina I). Convergence is a substrate, not shown to be the whole explanation.
cards.quote: When one cell hears from both skin and an internal organ, its firing alone does not say which one sent the signal.
cards.section: In the dorsal horn

cards.front: In the simplified gate control picture of the dorsal horn, how do large touch fibres and small nociceptor fibres each act on the inhibitory interneuron?
cards.back: Large fibres excite it, strengthening its damping of the transmission cell. Small fibres suppress it, weakening the damping. Both also excite the transmission cell directly.
cards.why: So rubbing reduces pain only if the damping that touch recruits outweighs its direct excitation of the transmission cell.
cards.quote: Large fibres excite it, so they strengthen the damping. Small fibres suppress it, so they weaken the damping.
cards.section: The gate in the dorsal horn

cards.front: In the simplified gate control picture, the inhibitory interneuron is removed. What does a light touch now do?
cards.back: It can send a signal up the pain line. Nothing damps the touch input, so touch alone can drive the transmission cell, a route to allodynia.
cards.quote: Touch alone can now drive the transmission cell, so a light touch could send a signal up the pain line.
cards.section: The gate in the dorsal horn

cards.front: Which part of the 1965 gate control theory survived, and which part is not settled?
cards.back: The general claim survived: the dorsal horn computes rather than passing signals straight through. The original wiring, with substantia gelatinosa cells inhibiting the afferent terminals themselves, is not settled.
cards.quote: What survived is the general claim: the dorsal horn computes, rather than passing signals straight through.
cards.section: The gate in the dorsal horn

cards.front: In mice, genetically ablating spinal inhibitory neurons of the dynorphin lineage made light touch evoke pain-like withdrawal. What does this show, and what does it not prove?
cards.back: These neurons are required to gate mechanical pain, as the gate picture predicts when inhibition is lost. It does not prove the 1965 diagram as drawn, and a withdrawing paw is a protective reflex, not proof of what the mouse feels.
cards.quote: Removing inhibitory neurons of the dynorphin lineage made light touch evoke pain-like withdrawal, a behavioural sign of mechanical allodynia.
cards.section: The gate in the dorsal horn

cards.front: Name the descending route by which the brainstem turns dorsal horn pain transmission up or down.
cards.back: The periaqueductal gray (PAG) of the midbrain supplies top-down input to the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM), which projects to the dorsal horn.
cards.quote: The periaqueductal gray (PAG), the grey matter around the midbrain's fluid canal, supplies top-down input to the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM)
cards.section: From the brainstem

cards.front: In a rodent, a drug makes RVM OFF cells fire continuously and silences RVM ON cells. Predict the effect on pain-related processing.
cards.back: It is turned down. OFF cells suppress and ON cells facilitate pain-related processing, so more OFF and less ON activity damps it.
cards.why: ON cells burst and OFF cells pause just before withdrawal from noxious heat; the classes are defined by that firing pattern.
cards.quote: OFF cells suppress and ON cells facilitate pain-related processing.
cards.section: From the brainstem

cards.front: In mice, activating GABAergic RVM projections to the dorsal horn facilitated mechanical nociception. How can an inhibitory projection turn pain up?
cards.back: By inhibiting an inhibitor. These projections inhibited enkephalin- and GABA-releasing dorsal horn interneurons, removing their brake. The sign of a transmitter does not give the sign of its effect.
cards.quote: An inhibitory projection turned the report up by inhibiting an inhibitor.
cards.section: From the brainstem

cards.front: Suppose a descending projection instead excites the dorsal horn interneurons that release enkephalin and GABA. Predict its effect on mechanical nociception.
cards.back: It should turn the report down. Exciting those inhibitory interneurons strengthens their brake on transmission.
cards.why: Rests on the GABAergic RVM result, where inhibiting these interneurons facilitated mechanical nociception: the effect's sign follows the target, not the transmitter.
cards.quote: The sign of a transmitter does not give the sign of its effect.
cards.section: From the brainstem

cards.front: In the thermal grill, interleaved warm and cool bars, neither painful alone, can feel like burning. What does this suggest about labelled lines?
cards.back: Some sensations seem to come from comparing lines, so labelled lines are a first approximation, not the whole code.
cards.quote: In the thermal grill, interleaved warm and cool bars, neither painful alone, can feel like burning.
cards.section: Where the idea stops

cards.front: Light touch hurts after a nerve injury, yet recordings show the skin's nerve endings are not sensitized. Which two spinal mechanisms from the lesson could help explain this?
cards.back: Loss of spinal inhibition can let touch input drive a pain line; central sensitization can raise the excitability and synaptic efficacy of central nociceptive neurons. These are candidate spinal explanations, not a unique localization from the recordings.
cards.why: Allodynia can arise at the ending or in the cord, and normal endings do not rule out altered descending control of dorsal-horn transmission.
cards.quote: It can arise from changes at the ending or in the cord.
cards.section: Where the idea stops

cards.front: A TRPV1 knockout mouse shows only a partial heat deficit. A later mouse study found acute heat withdrawal largely lost only when TRPV1, TRPM3 and TRPA1 were all removed. How do the two results fit together?
cards.back: Acute heat sensing appears distributed across several TRP channels, so removing TRPV1 alone leaves the others to carry much of the response, giving a partial deficit.
cards.why: Rests on the necessity rule: a gene can be needed for part of a response without being the only sensor.
cards.quote: Acute heat sensing appears to be distributed across several TRP channels.
cards.section: Heat sensing beyond TRPV1

cards.front: Piezo2 is needed for gentle touch in mice, yet Piezo2-knockout mouse sensory neurons still respond robustly to noxious pinch. What does this imply, and how does it parallel TRPV1 and heat?
cards.back: Something else also senses pinch, although in mice Piezo2 contributes to part of the response to painful mechanical stimuli. Like TRPV1 for heat, one channel can be needed for part of a modality without being its only sensor.
cards.quote: Something else also senses pinch, although in mice Piezo2 contributes to part of the response to painful mechanical stimuli
cards.section: Piezo2 and painful touch
